What I did:
- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - Security context: matched the stable deployment (no special settings)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged to match current traffic port)

Result:
- With 2 replicas on each deployment, the Service will send roughly 50/50 traffic between stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1).

How to verify:
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy,pods -l app=recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Send a few test requests and check headers/body or pod logs to confirm both versions are serving.

Adjusting traffic split (if needed):
- Scale replicas to change the ratio. Example ~75/25 toward stable:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-0 --replicas=6
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=2

Rollback options:
- Point Service back to only stable by restoring selector:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns patch svc recommendation-engine -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"recommendation-engine","version":"v2.0"}}}'
- Or scale canary to 0:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=0

Tell me if you want me to pin an exact traffic percentage via Ingress/Service Mesh weighting instead of replica-based approximation.

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I did:
- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - Security context: matched the stable deployment (no special settings)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged to match current traffic port)

Result:
- With 2 replicas on each deployment, the Service will send roughly 50/50 traffic between stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1).

How to verify:
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy,pods -l app=recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Send a few test requests and check headers/body or pod logs to confirm both versions are serving.

Adjusting traffic split (if needed):
- Scale replicas to change the ratio. Example ~75/25 toward stable:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-0 --replicas=6
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=2

Rollback options:
- Point Service back to only stable by restoring selector:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns patch svc recommendation-engine -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"recommendation-engine","version":"v2.0"}}}'
- Or scale canary to 0:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=0

Tell me if you want me to pin an exact traffic percentage via Ingress/Service Mesh weighting instead of replica-based approximation.

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29

  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1

  - Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged to match current traffic port)

Result:
- With 2 replicas on each deployment, the Service will send roughly 50/50 traffic between stable (v2.0) and canary (v2.1).

How to verify:
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy,pods -l app=recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Send a few test requests and check headers/body or pod logs to confirm both versions are serving.

Adjusting traffic split (if needed):
- Scale replicas to change the ratio. Example ~75/25 toward stable:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-0 --replicas=6
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=2

Rollback options:
- Point Service back to only stable by restoring selector:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns patch svc recommendation-engine -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"recommendation-engine","version":"v2.0"}}}'
- Or scale canary to 0:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=0

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The container was started with command/args ["/bin/sh", "-c"] and "nonexistent_command", causing a CrashLoopBackOff.
- Change made: Updated the Deployment to start nginx in the foreground.
  - command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
  - args: ["nginx -g 'daemon off;'"]
- Result: Deployment app in crashloop-test is healthy.
  - Replicas available: 1/1
  - Pod is Running and Ready.

If you’d prefer to rely on the image’s default entrypoint instead, I can remove the custom command/args entirely.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc". That left the claim unbound, so the pod couldn’t be scheduled.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since no volume was bound yet).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using an existing StorageClass: standard (the cluster’s default on your setup).
- The external provisioner created a volume and bound it to the PVC.

Current status
- homepage-pod in homepage-ns is Running and Ready (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster.
- PVC homepage-pvc is Bound via StorageClass standard.

How you can verify
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=homepage-pvc

If you prefer to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or need a different access mode/size, tell me and I’ll update the PVC accordingly.

I fixed it.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc". That left the claim unbound, so the pod couldn’t be scheduled.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since no volume was bound yet).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using an existing StorageClass: standard (the cluster’s default on your setup).
- The external provisioner created a volume and bound it to the PVC.

Current status
- homepage-pod in homepage-ns is Running and Ready (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster.
- PVC homepage-pvc is Bound via StorageClass standard.

How you can verify
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=homepage-pvc

If you prefer to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or need a different access mode/size, tell me and I’ll update the PVC accordingly.

I found the issue and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The container image (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but your probes and Service were using port 80.
- Liveness/readiness probes also pointed to non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing the pod to flap and never become ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.
- Left Service port exposed as 80 inside the cluster (Service port 80 -> container 8080).

Current status
- Deployment webapp is Available (1/1).
- Pod is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are healthy and pointing to the pod on port 8080.

Do you need external access?
- There’s no Ingress configured. If you want it reachable from outside the cluster, tell me the hostname you want and I can create an Ingress. Alternatively, I can expose it as a LoadBalancer (cloud permitting).
- For a quick test from your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80, then browse http://localhost:8080/

If you intended the app to serve on port 80 or have custom health endpoints, share those details and I can adjust accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
I found the issue and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The container image (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but your probes and Service were using port 80.
- Liveness/readiness probes also pointed to non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing the pod to flap and never become ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.
- Left Service port exposed as 80 inside the cluster (Service port 80 -> container 8080).

Current status
- Deployment webapp is Available (1/1).
- Pod is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are healthy and pointing to the pod on port 8080.

Do you need external access?
- There’s no Ingress configured. If you want it reachable from outside the cluster, tell me the hostname you want and I can create an Ingress. Alternatively, I can expose it as a LoadBalancer (cloud permitting).
- For a quick test from your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80, then browse http://localhost:8080/

If you intended the app to serve on port 80 or have custom health endpoints, share those details and I can adjust accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. Pods live in the core API group (""), so the SA had no permission to list them.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
  - Kept your existing apps/deployments list rule as-is.
- Your RoleBinding pod-reader-binding was already correct (binding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to Role/pod-reader-role in the same namespace).

How to verify
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Expected: yes
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Should list pods successfully.

If you ever need to read pods across all namespaces, use a ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. Pods live in the core API group (""), so the SA had no permission to list them.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
  - Kept your existing apps/deployments list rule as-is.
- Your RoleBinding pod-reader-binding was already correct (binding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to Role/pod-reader-role in the same namespace).

How to verify
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Expected: yes
- kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Should list pods successfully.

If you ever need to read pods across all namespaces, use a ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding instead.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service’s selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pod labels: app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints for Service nginx were empty, so the Service had no backends.
- The Service targetPort was wrong:
  - Service targetPort: 80
  - NGINX (unprivileged image) listens on: 8080
  - Result: Even with a matching selector, traffic would not reach the container.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service web/nginx to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Current status (verified)
- Endpoints now show the pod backend: 10.244.0.45:8080
- ClusterIP: 10.109.60.240:80 responds with the NGINX welcome page from within the cluster.

How you can verify
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
  - Should show PORT(S): 80/TCP and selector app=nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
  - Should list 10.244.0.45:8080 (or your pod IP:8080)
- From inside the cluster, curl http://10.109.60.240 should return the NGINX welcome page.

Do you need external access?
- Right now this is a ClusterIP Service (internal-only).
- Options if you want outside-cluster access:
  1) NodePort
     - I can switch the Service to type: NodePort (e.g., nodePort 30080) so you can reach http://<nodeIP>:30080.
  2) Ingress
     - If you have an Ingress controller, I can create an Ingress host (e.g., nginx.example.com) routing to this Service on port 80.
  3) Port-forward (for quick testing)
     - kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080

Tell me which exposure method you prefer and any hostname/port requirements, and I’ll set it up.

  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

  selector:

    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%

        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      nodeSelector: {}
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      nodeSelector: {}
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

Root cause
- Your Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Pods were Pending with FailedScheduling, so the Service had no endpoints. Calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local therefore hit an empty Service and resulted in connection refused.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-t4dmv: Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-whpxt: Running
- Service endpoints:
  - web-app-service -> 10.244.0.47:80, 10.244.0.48:80

This should restore connectivity for your frontend to web-app-service.

Notes and options
- If you intended to run this only on GPU nodes, either:
  - Label the target node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Or adjust the nodeSelector to match actual labels on your GPU nodes.
  - I can revert the change and set the proper labels/selectors if you confirm the desired constraint.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe on port 80 so traffic only routes when the app is ready.

Want me to add a readinessProbe and/or enforce the correct node labels/selectors as you prefer?

All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC (users and service accounts), resource quotas, and network policies. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy targeting and isolation (env/team/tenant, plus kubernetes.io/metadata.name for namespace selectors)

RBAC
- Per-developer admin within their own namespace:
  - Role namespace-owner (full access) in each of dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - RoleBindings binding each user (alice, bob, charlie) and their SA (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to namespace-owner in their own namespace
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs to ClusterRole view
- staging and prod:
  - No developer permissions granted; by default only cluster-admins (or whitelisted admins you bind) can access

Service Accounts
- Created in each dev namespace: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access to dev-shared

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10
  - Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20
  - Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50
  - Services: 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-* , dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Per-namespace allowances:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace traffic for each namespace
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system) from all created namespaces (covers “DNS and system services” for DNS)
- Developer egress scoped:
  - dev namespaces can egress only to:
    - same namespace
    - dev-shared (explicit allow to namespace dev-shared)
    - DNS in kube-system
  - dev-shared allows ingress only from dev namespaces labeled env=dev and tenant=developer
- staging/prod isolation:
  - default deny + no egress allows from dev namespaces ensure no dev↔staging/prod traffic
  - staging/prod still have DNS egress to kube-system; otherwise isolated

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC in a namespace: kubectl -n dev-alice get role,rolebinding
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota dev-ns-quota
- Network policies: kubectl -n dev-alice get netpol
- Test SA tokens (K8s 1.24+): kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
- Connectivity checks (example): run a temporary pod and curl between namespaces to confirm only allowed paths work

Notes and next steps (optional)
- If you want default CPU/memory requests and per-container limits, add a LimitRange in each namespace.
- If developers should also reach other cluster “system services” beyond DNS (e.g., a shared registry or logging in kube-system), we can add targeted egress rules to those Services/ports.
- Ensure your identity provider maps users “alice”, “bob”, “charlie” to Kubernetes User identities as referenced in the RoleBindings, or switch to group-based bindings if you prefer.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC (users and service accounts), resource quotas, and network policies. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy targeting and isolation (env/team/tenant, plus kubernetes.io/metadata.name for namespace selectors)

RBAC
- Per-developer admin within their own namespace:
  - Role namespace-owner (full access) in each of dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - RoleBindings binding each user (alice, bob, charlie) and their SA (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to namespace-owner in their own namespace
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs to ClusterRole view
- staging and prod:
  - No developer permissions granted; by default only cluster-admins (or whitelisted admins you bind) can access

Service Accounts
- Created in each dev namespace: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access to dev-shared

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10
  - Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20
  - Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50
  - Services: 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-* , dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Per-namespace allowances:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace traffic for each namespace
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system) from all created namespaces (covers “DNS and system services” for DNS)
- Developer egress scoped:
  - dev namespaces can egress only to:
    - same namespace
    - dev-shared (explicit allow to namespace dev-shared)
    - DNS in kube-system
  - dev-shared allows ingress only from dev namespaces labeled env=dev and tenant=developer
- staging/prod isolation:
  - default deny + no egress allows from dev namespaces ensure no dev↔staging/prod traffic
  - staging/prod still have DNS egress to kube-system; otherwise isolated

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC in a namespace: kubectl -n dev-alice get role,rolebinding
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota dev-ns-quota
- Network policies: kubectl -n dev-alice get netpol
- Test SA tokens (K8s 1.24+): kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
- Connectivity checks (example): run a temporary pod and curl between namespaces to confirm only allowed paths work

Notes and next steps (optional)
- If you want default CPU/memory requests and per-container limits, add a LimitRange in each namespace.
- If developers should also reach other cluster “system services” beyond DNS (e.g., a shared registry or logging in kube-system), we can add targeted egress rules to those Services/ports.
- Ensure your identity provider maps users “alice”, “bob”, “charlie” to Kubernetes User identities as referenced in the RoleBindings, or switch to group-based bindings if you prefer.

All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC (users and service accounts), resource quotas, and network policies. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for policy targeting and isolation (env/team/tenant, plus kubernetes.io/metadata.name for namespace selectors)

RBAC
- Per-developer admin within their own namespace:
  - Role namespace-owner (full access) in each of dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
  - RoleBindings binding each user (alice, bob, charlie) and their SA (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to namespace-owner in their own namespace
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs to ClusterRole view
- staging and prod:
  - No developer permissions granted; by default only cluster-admins (or whitelisted admins you bind) can access

Service Accounts
- Created in each dev namespace: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access to dev-shared

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10
  - Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20
  - Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50
  - Services: 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-* , dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Per-namespace allowances:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits intra-namespace traffic for each namespace
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system) from all created namespaces (covers “DNS and system services” for DNS)
- Developer egress scoped:
  - dev namespaces can egress only to:
    - same namespace
    - dev-shared (explicit allow to namespace dev-shared)
    - DNS in kube-system
  - dev-shared allows ingress only from dev namespaces labeled env=dev and tenant=developer
- staging/prod isolation:
  - default deny + no egress allows from dev namespaces ensure no dev↔staging/prod traffic
  - staging/prod still have DNS egress to kube-system; otherwise isolated

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC in a namespace: kubectl -n dev-alice get role,rolebinding
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota dev-ns-quota
- Network policies: kubectl -n dev-alice get netpol
- Test SA tokens (K8s 1.24+): kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
- Connectivity checks (example): run a temporary pod and curl between namespaces to confirm only allowed paths work

Notes and next steps (optional)
- If you want default CPU/memory requests and per-container limits, add a LimitRange in each namespace.
- If developers should also reach other cluster “system services” beyond DNS (e.g., a shared registry or logging in kube-system), we can add targeted egress rules to those Services/ports.
- Ensure your identity provider maps users “alice”, “bob”, “charlie” to Kubernetes User identities as referenced in the RoleBindings, or switch to group-based bindings if you prefer.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and did for VirtualMachine vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm:

Root cause
- The VM references a cloud-init secret that did not exist. The virt-launcher pod failed to mount the cloud-init volume:
  - Event: FailedMount: "secret 'vm-cloud-init' not found" (volume "cloudinit-udata")
- This prevented the pod from initializing and the VMI from starting.

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal valid cloud-init content.
  - Keys: userData and userdata (base64 for "#cloud-config")
- Restarted the VM to re-trigger provisioning.

Outcome (success)
- Successful: Yes.
- Post-fix vm-troubleshoot shows:
  - VM printableStatus: Running, Ready=True
  - VMI phase: Running, Ready=True
  - virt-launcher pod: Running and ContainersReady=True
  - Network: IP assigned (e.g., 10.244.0.79)
  - Events: “VirtualMachineInstance started.” and pod Started/Ready events present
- Note: virt-launcher logs also show “kvm not present. Using software emulation.” This is informational (performance will be lower) but not blocking.

What you might want to do next
- Replace the placeholder cloud-init userData with your desired configuration in the vm-cloud-init secret. If you provide the intended cloud-init content, I can update the secret for you.

Steps.message: VM created with missing Secret reference - waiting for failure state

Here’s what I found and did for VirtualMachine vm-test-troubleshoot/broken-vm:

Root cause
- The VM references a cloud-init secret that did not exist. The virt-launcher pod failed to mount the cloud-init volume:
  - Event: FailedMount: "secret 'vm-cloud-init' not found" (volume "cloudinit-udata")
- This prevented the pod from initializing and the VMI from starting.

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in namespace vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal valid cloud-init content.
  - Keys: userData and userdata (base64 for "#cloud-config")
- Restarted the VM to re-trigger provisioning.

Outcome (success)
- Successful: Yes.
- Post-fix vm-troubleshoot shows:
  - VM printableStatus: Running, Ready=True
  - VMI phase: Running, Ready=True
  - virt-launcher pod: Running and ContainersReady=True
  - Network: IP assigned (e.g., 10.244.0.79)
  - Events: “VirtualMachineInstance started.” and pod Started/Ready events present
- Note: virt-launcher logs also show “kvm not present. Using software emulation.” This is informational (performance will be lower) but not blocking.

What you might want to do next
- Replace the placeholder cloud-init userData with your desired configuration in the vm-cloud-init secret. If you provide the intended cloud-init content, I can update the secret for you.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData runs an immediate shutdown. Because the VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, KubeVirt continuously recreates the VMI after each shutdown, resulting in a crashloop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In the NoCloud userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd contains: shutdown -h now

How to fix it
- Preferred: Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init so the guest doesn’t power off right after boot.
  - Edit the VM and update spec.template.spec.volumes[name=cloudinit].cloudInitNoCloud.userData, removing the runcmd entry that contains “shutdown -h now”.
  - Restart the VM after updating the spec.
- If you intentionally want the guest to shut down after boot, change the VM’s runStrategy so it doesn’t auto-restart:
  - Set spec.runStrategy to Halted (or Manual), then start the VM only when needed.
  
Either change stops the restart loop; removing the shutdown command is the usual fix if the VM is meant to stay running.

Steps.message: Waiting for VM to attempt boot and crash...

Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData runs an immediate shutdown. Because the VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, KubeVirt continuously recreates the VMI after each shutdown, resulting in a crashloop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In the NoCloud userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd contains: shutdown -h now

How to fix it
- Preferred: Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init so the guest doesn’t power off right after boot.
  - Edit the VM and update spec.template.spec.volumes[name=cloudinit].cloudInitNoCloud.userData, removing the runcmd entry that contains “shutdown -h now”.
  - Restart the VM after updating the spec.
- If you intentionally want the guest to shut down after boot, change the VM’s runStrategy so it doesn’t auto-restart:
  - Set spec.runStrategy to Halted (or Manual), then start the VM only when needed.
  
Either change stops the restart loop; removing the shutdown command is the usual fix if the VM is meant to stay running.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s the diagnosis for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm:

Root cause
- The VM’s cloud-init userData runs an immediate shutdown. Because the VM is configured with runStrategy: Always, KubeVirt continuously recreates the VMI after each shutdown, resulting in a crashloop.

Problematic cloud-init command
- In the NoCloud userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd contains: shutdown -h now

How to fix it
- Preferred: Remove the shutdown command from cloud-init so the guest doesn’t power off right after boot.
  - Edit the VM and update spec.template.spec.volumes[name=cloudinit].cloudInitNoCloud.userData, removing the runcmd entry that contains “shutdown -h now”.
  - Restart the VM after updating the spec.
- If you intentionally want the guest to shut down after boot, change the VM’s runStrategy so it doesn’t auto-restart:
  - Set spec.runStrategy to Halted (or Manual), then start the VM only when needed.
  
Either change stops the restart loop; removing the shutdown command is the usual fix if the VM is meant to stay running.

results.taskOutput:
I tried to retrieve guest-agent data from VM test-vm-with-agent in namespace vm-test-guest-info, but the guest agent is not yet connected. Server response: “VMI does not have guest agent connected.” As a result, OS, filesystem, network, and users data are currently unavailable.

Why this can happen
- The VM is still booting or cloud-init is still running, delaying the agent start.
- qemu-guest-agent service is installed but not started/enabled yet.
- The VM is missing the virtio serial channel for the agent (org.qemu.guest_agent.0) in its spec.

What guest agent data will include once available
- Operating system
  - Hostname
  - OS name/distribution and version
  - Kernel version
  - Architecture
  - Uptime
  - Timezone
- Filesystems
  - Device and mount point (e.g., /dev/vda1 mounted on /)
  - Filesystem type (ext4, xfs, etc.)
  - Capacity/used/available bytes
  - Inode usage
- Network interfaces
  - Interface name (eth0, ens3, etc.)
  - MAC address
  - IPv4/IPv6 addresses
  - MTU
  - State (up/down)
- Logged-in users
  - Username
  - TTY/terminal
  - Host/source
  - Login time and idle

How to get the agent connected quickly (inside the VM)
- Check cloud-init status: cloud-init status --wait (or tail -f /var/log/cloud-init.log)
- Verify/install agent:
  - Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y qemu-guest-agent
  - RHEL/CentOS/Fedora: sudo dnf install -y qemu-guest-agent
- Start and enable service: sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
- Verify virtio channel present: ls -l /dev/virtio-ports/org.qemu.guest_agent.0
- Confirm service running: systemctl status qemu-guest-agent

KubeVirt-side checks
- Ensure the VM spec includes a virtio-serial channel for org.qemu.guest_agent.0.
- Check the VMI conditions for AgentConnected to become True.

Would you like me to retry fetching the guest-agent information now or in a couple of minutes?

I tried to retrieve guest-agent data from VM test-vm-with-agent in namespace vm-test-guest-info, but the guest agent is not yet connected. Server response: “VMI does not have guest agent connected.” As a result, OS, filesystem, network, and users data are currently unavailable.

Why this can happen
- The VM is still booting or cloud-init is still running, delaying the agent start.
- qemu-guest-agent service is installed but not started/enabled yet.
- The VM is missing the virtio serial channel for the agent (org.qemu.guest_agent.0) in its spec.

What guest agent data will include once available
- Operating system
  - Hostname
  - OS name/distribution and version
  - Kernel version
  - Architecture
  - Uptime
  - Timezone
- Filesystems
  - Device and mount point (e.g., /dev/vda1 mounted on /)
  - Filesystem type (ext4, xfs, etc.)
  - Capacity/used/available bytes
  - Inode usage
- Network interfaces
  - Interface name (eth0, ens3, etc.)
  - MAC address
  - IPv4/IPv6 addresses
  - MTU
  - State (up/down)
- Logged-in users
  - Username
  - TTY/terminal
  - Host/source
  - Login time and idle

How to get the agent connected quickly (inside the VM)
- Check cloud-init status: cloud-init status --wait (or tail -f /var/log/cloud-init.log)
- Verify/install agent:
  - Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y qemu-guest-agent
  - RHEL/CentOS/Fedora: sudo dnf install -y qemu-guest-agent
- Start and enable service: sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
- Verify virtio channel present: ls -l /dev/virtio-ports/org.qemu.guest_agent.0
- Confirm service running: systemctl status qemu-guest-agent

KubeVirt-side checks
- Ensure the VM spec includes a virtio-serial channel for org.qemu.guest_agent.0.
- Check the VMI conditions for AgentConnected to become True.

Would you like me to retry fetching the guest-agent information now or in a couple of minutes?
